Manoj, a second-year student in Dharwad, walked twenty minutes each way to college to save the auto fare. He argued with the canteen boy over two rupees for extra chutney and skipped tea most days.

Then his scholarship refund came through, a lump sum he hadn't expected. That same evening he bought a fancy watch at the market, took his friend Chetan out for a big dinner, and ordered new speakers.

"You walked in the heat all month to save ten rupees," Chetan said, "and now this?"

"That was my daily money," Manoj said. "This is extra."

At the end of the month, his phone bill came. He looked at his almost empty account and felt a jolt of panic. The watch ticked on his wrist.

qa.q: What did Manoj buy at the market the evening the refund came?
qa.a: He bought a fancy watch.

qa.q: Why did spending the refund freely feel reasonable to Manoj?
qa.a: He felt excited and carefree because the refund seemed like "extra" money, separate from the daily money he guarded so tightly.

qa.q: What would you advise Manoj to do the next time a refund arrives?
qa.a: He could look at all his money together before spending and talk it over with a parent or a college finance adviser.

qa.q: How does Chetan see Manoj's spending?
qa.a: Chetan is surprised and a little puzzled that Manoj pinches rupees daily but spends a big sum in one evening.

grounding: A student spends a refund carelessly while pinching on small daily costs, keeping money in separate mental pots.

In Buenos Aires, Santiago worked weekends at a café while studying engineering. He brought lunch from home every day and refused to buy a coffee on campus, even when he was exhausted.

In December the café gave him a holiday bonus. Within a week, he'd spent it on concert tickets, a new jacket, and a weekend trip with friends.

His flatmate Soo-ah watched him refuse a coffee again in January. "You spent your whole bonus in a week, but you won't buy a coffee?"

"The bonus was fun money," Santiago said. "Coffee comes out of my real money."

"It's all your money," Soo-ah said.

Santiago opened his banking app and looked at the total. It was lower than he'd thought, and he felt a little sick.

qa.q: Where did Santiago work on weekends?
qa.a: He worked weekends at a café.

qa.q: How did Santiago feel when he looked at his total in January?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little sick, realising his separate "fun" and "real" money were one smaller pile.

qa.q: What could Santiago try so he sees his whole picture?
qa.a: He could look at all his money in one place each month and, if unsure, ask a trusted adult or a bank adviser about choices.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see Santiago's split between fun money and real money?
qa.a: Soo-ah finds it confusing and a bit worrying, since to her it's all the same money.

grounding: A student spends a bonus freely while pinching on daily costs, keeping separate mental accounts that hide his real picture.

Parul, you're nervous about training the new girl in your team? Let your Lalremsiami aunty tell you about my first year as a supervisor in Aizawl, when I was twenty-six.

We hired a young woman fresh from college. On her first day, I gave her everything: every file, every rule, every name. By evening her eyes were red. I thought she was just shy.

The next day I watched her again. She wrote down everything I said, then looked at the notes, lost. I realised I'd poured a whole river into one cup.

The science club had only fifteen minutes before the bell, and the projector kept flickering. Ms Ankita played a short video of children passing a ball. "Count the passes by the team in white," she said.

Harish, eleven, leaned forward. One, two, three. The screen flickered. He kept counting hard. Eleven, twelve.

"Fourteen!" he called.

"Good. Did anyone see the man in the bear costume?"

Harish laughed. "What bear?"

She played it again. A man in a bear costume walked right through the middle, waved, and walked off.

Harish's jaw dropped. "That wasn't there!"

"It was," Ms Ankita said. "You were looking at the ball. Your eyes saw it, but your attention didn't."

qa.q: What did Ms Ankita ask the children to count?
qa.a: The passes by the team in white.

qa.q: Why did Harish say "That wasn't there!"?
qa.a: He felt shocked and a bit disbelieving, because he was so focused on counting that he truly didn't notice the bear.

qa.q: What lesson could Harish take from the video?
qa.a: When he focuses hard on one thing, he may miss others, so for important things he could check twice or ask others what they saw.

qa.q: How might Ms Ankita feel seeing the children's reactions?
qa.a: Ms Ankita probably feels pleased and amused that the experiment worked even with a flickering projector.

grounding: A child counting passes in a video doesn't notice a surprising figure crossing the screen, as attention decides what is seen.
